summary.text: Rational Taylor bounds, together with the standard harmonic upper and lower approximations to Euler’s constant, give \(16/9<e^\gamma<41/23\); they also show \(1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\), using general exponential estimates for large \(n\) and finite checks for the initial cases, so the relevant floor increment is always 1 or 2. Telescoping these floor increments and using \(e^{H_{N+1}}/N\to e^\gamma\) yields limiting normalized counts \(e^\gamma-1\) and \(2-e^\gamma\), hence ratio \((e^\gamma-1)/(2-e^\gamma)\), whose stated bounds follow from the rational bounds on \(e^\gamma\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k
\]
be the \(n\)-th harmonic sum, and let \(\gamma\) denote the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Put
\[
E=e^\gamma.
\]
We will prove that the limiting ratio in the conjecture is
\[
L=\frac{E-1}{2-E},
\]
and that \(7/2<L<18/5\).

First we express the ranks in a convenient form. The logarithmic terms preceding \(H_n\) are those \(\log(k+1)\), with \(k\geq 1\), for which
\[
\log(k+1)<H_n,
\]
equivalently \(k+1<e^{H_n}\). Their number is \(\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\). (There is no equality between a harmonic sum and one of these logarithms: a positive rational harmonic sum cannot be the logarithm of an integer, since the exponential of a nonzero algebraic number is transcendental.) There are also exactly \(n\) harmonic sums \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\) up to and including \(H_n\). Thus the rank is
\[
a(n)=n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
The floor here is nonnegative, so this agrees with viewing it as either a natural-number floor or an integer floor. In particular, if
\[
d_n=a(n+1)-a(n),
\]
then
\[
d_n=1+\lfloor e^{H_{n+1}}-1\rfloor-\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor. \tag{2}
\]
We shall apply this for \(n\geq1\).

## 1. Bounds for \(e^\gamma\)

We need the explicit enclosure
\[
\frac{16}{9}<E<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{3}
\]
Here is how it is obtained.

Consider the standard lower and upper approximants
\[
\alpha_n=H_n-\log(n+1),\qquad
\beta_n=H_n-\log n\quad(n\geq1).
\]
The sequence \(\alpha_n\) is strictly increasing, \(\beta_n\) is strictly decreasing, and both tend to \(\gamma\). For completeness, these facts follow from
\[
\log(1+t)<t\quad(t>0)
\]
and
\[
\log(1+t)>\frac{t}{1+t}\quad(t>0).
\]
Indeed,
\[
\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n
 =\frac1{n+1}-\log\left(1+\frac1{n+1}\right)>0,
\]
whereas
\[
\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n
 =\frac1{n+1}-\log\left(1+\frac1n\right)<0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\beta_n-\alpha_n=\log\left(1+\frac1n\right)\longrightarrow0,
\]
so their common limit is \(\gamma\). Consequently, for every positive \(n\),
\[
H_n-\log(n+1)<\gamma<H_n-\log n. \tag{4}
\]

We use rational Taylor estimates for the exponential. For rational \(x\geq0\), define
\[
T_m(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{x^j}{j!}.
\]
Since all terms in the exponential series are nonnegative,
\[
T_m(x)\leq e^x. \tag{5}
\]
For \(0\leq x\leq1\) and \(m>0\), the usual exponential-series remainder estimate gives
\[
e^x\leq U_m(x):=T_m(x)+\frac{x^m(m+1)}{m!\,m}. \tag{6}
\]
This follows, for example, by bounding the absolute tail of the exponential series after the first \(m\) terms; under \(0\le x\le1\), the successive factorial denominators make the tail no larger than the displayed rational remainder.

All harmonic numbers involved below are rational, so the following are exact rational inequalities, checked by putting the finite sums over common denominators and cross-multiplying positive integers:
\[
\frac{16}{9}<\frac{T_8(H_{300}/8)^8}{301}, \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
\frac{U_{15}(H_{580}/8)^8}{580}<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{8}
\]
For orientation only, the middle quantities are approximately \(1.7780891687\) and \(1.7826080457\), respectively; the proof of (7) and (8) is the exact rational arithmetic just described. Also, direct summation gives \(0\leq H_{580}/8\leq1\), as required for (6).

By (5), positivity, and \((e^{H_{300}/8})^8=e^{H_{300}}\), inequality (7) yields
\[
\frac{16}{9}<\frac{e^{H_{300}}}{301}
 =e^{H_{300}-\log301}=e^{\alpha_{300}}<e^\gamma=E.
\]
Similarly, (6) and (8) give
\[
E=e^\gamma<e^{\beta_{580}}
 =\frac{e^{H_{580}}}{580}
 \leq\frac{U_{15}(H_{580}/8)^8}{580}<\frac{41}{23}.
\]
This proves (3).

## 2. Every increment of \(e^{H_n}\) lies strictly between 1 and 2

Since
\[
H_{n+1}=H_n+\frac1{n+1},
\]
we have the exact identity
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
=e^{H_n}\left(e^{1/(n+1)}-1\right). \tag{9}
\]

### Lower bound

For \(n\geq2\), the upper approximant in (4), together with (3), gives
\[
\gamma<H_n-\log n,
\]
and therefore
\[
e^{H_n}>nE>\frac{16n}{9}. \tag{10}
\]
The elementary inequality \(e^x\geq1+x\) gives
\[
e^{1/(n+1)}-1\geq\frac1{n+1}. \tag{11}
\]
Combining (9)–(11),
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}> rac{16n}{9(n+1)}\geq1,
\]
because \(16n\geq9(n+1)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence
\[
1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}\qquad(n\geq2). \tag{12}
\]

The remaining case \(n=1\) is handled by the same rational Taylor bounds. Exact rational arithmetic gives
\[
1<T_8(H_2/4)^4-U_8(H_1/4)^4. \tag{13}
\]
Here \(H_1/4\leq1\). By (5) and (6),
\[
T_8(H_2/4)^4\leq e^{H_2},
\qquad
e^{H_1}\leq U_8(H_1/4)^4.
\]
Thus (13) implies \(1<e^{H_2}-e^{H_1}\). Together with (12),
\[
1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{14}
\]

### Upper bound

We first treat \(n\geq8\). The lower approximant in (4), together with (3), gives
\[
H_n-\log(n+1)<\gamma,
\]
so
\[
e^{H_n}<(n+1)E<(n+1)\frac{41}{23}. \tag{15}
\]
For \(0\leq x\leq1\), we also have
\[
e^x-1\leq x+x^2. \tag{16}
\]
One way to see this directly from (6) is to use \(m=2\):
\[
e^x\leq1+x+\frac34x^2\leq1+x+x^2.
\]
Taking \(x=1/(n+1)\) in (16), and using (9) and (15), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
&< (n+1)\frac{41}{23}
 \left(\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{(n+1)^2}\right)\\
&=\frac{41}{23}\left(1+\frac1{n+1}\right)\\
&\leq\frac{41}{23}\left(1+\frac19\right)
 =\frac{410}{207}<2.
\end{aligned} \tag{17}
\]

It remains to treat \(1\leq n\leq7\). For each such \(n\), exact rational calculation gives
\[
U_8(H_{n+1}/4)^4-T_8(H_n/4)^4<2. \tag{18}
\]
The seven left sides, as decimal guides to the exact rational comparisons, are approximately
\[
1.763407255,\ 1.773012061,\ 1.776495013,\ 1.778131801,
\ 1.779030264,\ 1.779578680,\ 1.779941494.
\]
All are obtained from finite rational sums; (18) is established by common-denominator integer comparison. Since \(H_{n+1}/4\leq H_8/4<1\), the upper Taylor estimate applies. Thus
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}\leq U_8(H_{n+1}/4)^4,
\qquad
T_8(H_n/4)^4\leq e^{H_n},
\]
and (18) implies
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2.
\]
Combining these cases with (14), we have the fundamental estimate
\[
1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{19}
\]

## 3. Conversion to rank differences

We use a simple fact about floors. If real numbers \(x,y\) satisfy
\[
1<y-x<2,
\]
then
\[
0<\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor<3.
\]
Indeed, \(\lfloor y\rfloor\leq y<\lfloor y\rfloor+1\), and similarly for \(x\); combining these inequalities with the bounds on \(y-x\) gives the displayed strict bounds. Since the difference of floors is an integer, it must be either \(1\) or \(2\). Hence
\[
1+\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor\in\{2,3\}. \tag{20}
\]

Apply this with
\[
x=e^{H_n}-1,\qquad y=e^{H_{n+1}}-1.
\]
Condition (19) is exactly \(1<y-x<2\). Equation (2) and (20) therefore show that
\[
d_n\in\{2,3\}\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{21}
\]
This proves the first assertion of the conjecture.

## 4. Exact formulas for the numbers of 2s and 3s

For \(N\geq0\), let \(C_3(N)\) be the number of 3s among
\[
d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_N,
\]
and put \(C_2(N)=N-C_3(N)\). Because each \(d_n\) is either 2 or 3,
\[
C_3(N)=\sum_{n=1}^N(d_n-2). \tag{22}
\]

Summing (2) from \(n=1\) to \(N\), the floor terms telescope:
\[
\sum_{n=1}^N d_n
=N+\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor-\lfloor e^{H_1}-1\rfloor. \tag{23}
\]
Substituting (23) into (22) gives
\[
C_3(N)=\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor
       -\lfloor e^{H_1}-1\rfloor-N. \tag{24}
\]
Consequently,
\[
C_2(N)=2N-\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor
       +\lfloor e^{H_1}-1\rfloor. \tag{25}
\]

## 5. The limiting ratio

Since
\[
H_N-\log(N+1)\longrightarrow\gamma,
\]
continuity of the exponential gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_N}}{N+1}
=e^{H_N-\log(N+1)}\longrightarrow E. \tag{26}
\]
Replacing \(N\) by \(N+1\) in (26) yields
\[
\frac{e^{H_{N+1}}}{N+2}\longrightarrow E.
\]
Since \((N+2)/N\to1\), it follows that
\[
\frac{e^{H_{N+1}}}{N}\longrightarrow E. \tag{27}
\]

The floor changes the numerator by only a bounded amount. More precisely,
\[
e^{H_{N+1}}-2
<\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor
\leq e^{H_{N+1}}-1
\leq e^{H_{N+1}}.
\]
After division by \(N>0\), the lower and upper bounds both tend to \(E\), by (27) and \(2/N\to0\). Therefore
\[
\frac{\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor}{N}\longrightarrow E. \tag{28}
\]

Divide (24) by \(N\). The fixed term \(\lfloor e^{H_1}-1\rfloor/N\) tends to zero, so (28) gives
\[
\frac{C_3(N)}N\longrightarrow E-1. \tag{29}
\]
Similarly, either from (25) or from \(C_2(N)=N-C_3(N)\),
\[
\frac{C_2(N)}N\longrightarrow2-E. \tag{30}
\]
By (3), \(E<41/23<2\), so \(2-E>0\). In particular, (30) implies that \(C_2(N)>0\) for all sufficiently large \(N\). Thus the convention that the ratio is set to zero when \(C_2(N)=0\) has no effect on its limit. Dividing (29) by (30), we obtain
\[
\frac{C_3(N)}{C_2(N)}\longrightarrow
L:=\frac{E-1}{2-E}. \tag{31}
\]

Finally, the denominator \(2-E\) is positive. The lower bound in (3) is exactly what is needed for
\[
\frac{E-1}{2-E}>\frac72,
\]
because, after multiplying by the positive denominator, this inequality is equivalent to
\[
E-1>\frac72(2-E),
\]
or \(E>16/9\). Likewise,
\[
\frac{E-1}{2-E}<\frac{18}{5}
\]
is equivalent to
\[
E-1<\frac{18}{5}(2-E),
\]
or \(E<41/23\). Both are strict by (3). Therefore
\[
3.5<L<3.6,
\]
and (21) and (31) establish both parts of the conjecture.
